messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Stock Broker
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Idealized Families: Happy families, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Sorn

Sorn was thirty-eight years old when she came to the intake appointment, and she arrived precisely on time—a habit born from years of needing to know exactly where she was and when. She was a stock broker at a mid-sized firm in the financial district, a role that had once felt like proof of her capability, her worth, her control over her own life. That was before.

Three years ago, a man named David Reeves had become convinced he was in love with her. They had met once, briefly, at a networking event. She had been polite. He had interpreted this as invitation. What followed was eighteen months of escalating contact: emails that grew increasingly personal, then frantic; messages left on her work phone; appearances at her apartment building, sometimes at night. When she changed her number, he found her on social media. When she blocked him, he created new accounts. The police were involved, a restraining order was filed, and eventually he was arrested after he was found outside her apartment at two in the morning with a notebook containing detailed observations of her daily movements. The terror of that period—of never knowing when or where he would appear, of the violation of being watched, of his certainty that he knew her better than she knew herself—had been all-consuming.

Now, three years later, Sorn was still living in the aftermath of those eighteen months. The traumatic event itself had a quality of unreality that disturbed her. When she tried to recount it to her therapist, she found herself saying, "It sounds insane when I say it out loud. It sounds like something that happened to someone else. But it happened to me." The specificity of his observations—the exact times she left for work, the coffee shop she frequented on Thursdays, the color of her car—had been so meticulous, so detailed, that it had shattered her sense of privacy. Yet when she tried to hold the full weight of it in her mind, it felt too extreme, too cinematic. This disconnect was itself a torment: she knew intellectually that it had been real, but her mind seemed unwilling to accept the scale of the violation.

When the memory surfaced—and it did so without warning, triggered by ordinary moments in her day—the distinction between then and now collapsed entirely. A loud noise in the office, a car door slamming, a phone ringing with an unexpected caller ID, and suddenly she was back in that apartment, heart racing, convinced that he was there, that the restraining order had been lifted, that the police had made a mistake. The terror was identical to what she had felt in those months: the same electrical surge through her body, the same certainty that something catastrophic was about to happen. It did not feel like memory. It felt like present danger.

Alcohol smell was another trigger, though the connection was indirect. David had shown up at her building reeking of whiskey on several occasions, his speech slurred but his purpose clear. Now, when she caught the scent—at a restaurant, from a colleague's breath—her nervous system responded as if he were in the room. Her partner had begun to notice her flinching away from him after work drinks.

Most painful was her reaction to happy families. When she saw a couple with young children, or heard a friend describe their family dinner, something in her fractured. These scenes of safety, of belonging, of the assumption that you could build a life without it being invaded and contaminated by someone else's obsession, triggered a grief so acute it felt almost like the original terror. She had come to believe that such safety was an illusion, that vigilance and isolation were the only honest ways to live. Her own relationship, a three-year partnership with Marcus, had begun to suffer under the weight of her hypervigilance and her conviction that closeness itself was dangerous.

It was Marcus who had finally insisted she seek help. He had found her one morning sitting in the dark, unable to explain why, unable to move. She had called in sick to work for the third time that week. Her firm had begun to ask questions about her performance. She came to the appointment because staying as she was had become unsustainable, but she was terrified that talking about it would make it more real, not less.
